transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-10 15:00 PST | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Ethan Park, Maya Lin, Jonas Rivera (Redwood); Priya Nair, Marcus Li, Aisha Gomez (Arcadia)

Summary: High-level recap at top, see notes. Audio quality: medium, occasional brief dropouts and auto-transcription errors (KV cash, privatlink).

[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about an hour, so the plan is to walk through networking options for Private VPC and then dive into runtime impacts — batching, KV cache, quant — and then leave time for Q&A.
[00:18] Priya (Arcadia): Thanks, yea we want to understand PrivateLink vs peering, how NATs should be set up, DNS resolution across accounts, and most importantly how network design affects latency and throughput for our real-time triage workloads.
[00:34] Maya (Redwood SE): Great, I'll start with an architecture slide — imagine Redwood Private control plane in a customer-managed VPC. We support two primary connectivity patterns: VPC peering (or Transit Gateway) and AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints). Both have tradeoffs.
[00:50] Marcus: Quick question, is PrivateLink mandatory for Private deployments? We have strict egress rules and limited public endpoints.
[01:02] Ethan: Not mandatory, PrivateLink is an option. With PrivateLink you get interface ENIs in your subnet, traffic stays on the AWS backbone, you don’t need internet egress for control plane calls. Peering/Transit is another option but requires route table config across accounts.
[01:20] Aisha: Are there differences in latency? Peering vs PrivateLink?
[01:27] Maya: In our benchmarks PrivateLink is slightly higher latency (network hop/ENI) than peering, but variance is lower because it's a managed endpoint. Peering can be lower latency but depends on routing — if you cross regions or Transit, you may hit extra hops. For sub-100ms SLOs peering can be preferable if you control both sides and avoid NAT.
[01:45] Priya: Important: we route all outbound through an egress NAT/Proxy for auditing, so that could add jitter.
[01:53] Jonas (Redwood): Right, and that's a crucial runtime implication: KV cache locality and continuous batching assume low tail latency. If every token request is tied to an egressed control-plane call behind a NAT with TCP connection churn, you see increased p99. Two mitigation patterns: keep long lived connections within the VPC (PrivateLink or peering with internal IPs) or allow egress to Redwood endpoints via VPC endpoint with policy that allows only our IPs.
[02:20] Marcus: When you say KV cache locality, do you mean the model's KV cache for attention keys?
[02:26] Maya: Yes, kv cache — sometimes the transcription writes cash — but it's the same. KV cache is kept on the GPU side, but the inference runtime still needs occasional RPC calls for cache warmup or prefetch in multi-instance setups. If control-plane or metadata calls are slow, first-token latency suffers.
[02:45] Priya: Our compliance requires all control-plane traffic to flow through a managed proxy for logging, is Redwood compatible with proxying?
[02:52] Ethan: Yes, we support HTTP proxy + mTLS. For PrivateLink we can deploy interface endpoints and enforce endpoint policy plus TLS; we also support client certs for extra mTLS. We'll share sample proxy configs.
[03:10] [03:10] Maya: Let's run through a couple of network topologies — I'll talk through diagrams.
[03:14] Maya: Topology A: PrivateLink per region, each Redwood service exposed as an interface endpoint. Pros: no cross-account route table changes, fine-grained IAM policy, AWS-managed connectivity. Cons: slightly higher latency vs peering, and you pay per-ENI and per-AZ endpoint.
[03:34] Maya: Topology B: VPC Peering / Transit Gateway — single private network with direct routes. Pros: lowest network latency inside the VPC, simpler egress if you already have shared services. Cons: you need to manage route tables, and cross-account peering limits, transit costs.
[03:52] Priya: For us cost matters but security and auditability are top. We also want minimal variance in p99.
[03:59] Jonas: If p99 is critical consider peering inside the same AZs, and avoid NAT in the data path. Use NAT only for outbound to internet and keep service-to-service traffic internal.
[04:12] Marcus: How are DNS records handled? We use split-horizon and Route53 Resolver endpoints for internal lookups.
[04:19] Maya: We commonly recommend Route53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints. For PrivateLink you map the endpoint DNS to the interface IPs — we can also support conditional forwarding to your resolver. This avoids public DNS lookups and keeps your records internal.
[04:36] Priya: Do we need to change our existing zone names? We have internal zone arcadia.local.
[04:41] Ethan: No, you can keep internal names; you'll create alias or CNAME mappings or endpoint-specific records — we'll provide an example.
[04:50] Aisha: What about NAT gateway scale and burst? We already saw NAT saturate on heavy egress. Does that affect inference traffic?
[04:58] Maya: If control-plane or fetch calls route through the NAT, heavy egress can increase latency. For large token throughput spikes, prefer keeping model RPC traffic internal and use NAT only for telemetry and optional downloads. If you must use NAT, ensure autoscaling NAT or use multiple NAT gateways per AZ.
[05:20] Priya: Let's switch to runtime perf. We want to understand batching, KV cache effects, and quantization choices for our 2k token median queries.
[05:30] Jonas: I'll cover batching. Redwood runtime supports continuous batching and dynamic batching. For high QPS with small requests, batching increases GPU utilization dramatically and reduces cost per token, but increases median latency somewhat. We tune the max_batch_size and latency floor to meet SLO.
[05:48] Marcus: Do you expose the batching parameters to us? We want to lock latency at 50-100ms median.
[05:55] Maya: Yes, you can set per-route profiles. In Dedicated or Private deployments you can pin batch configs per model route. We recommend starting with max_batch_size=8 and latency_floor_ms=50 for the 2k token workload, but we'll tune during the benchmark.
[06:12] Priya: KV cache warm vs cold — how much does that change latency for the first token?
[06:18] Jonas: Cold KV starts cost you an extra setup step depending on model and serving topology. If you have prefix caching or reuse across sessions, p50/p95 improves. First token can be 10-50ms slower depending on model size and prefetch strategy.
[06:34] Maya: Also quantization: int8 or lvq quant affects throughput and sometimes increases CPU/GPU memory locality. Lower precision usually reduces latency for large batch throughput but can increase small-batch variability. For latency-sensitive workloads we sometimes recommend mixed precision with quantized weights for throughput and fp16 paths for single-token low-latency requests.
[06:58] Priya: Can we toggle quantization per route?
[07:01] Ethan: Yes, per-model variant. You can pin a specific quantized artifact for one route and a fp16 variant for another; runtime will route based on policy.
[07:09] Marcus: How do you handle fallbacks if a quantized variant fails quality? Is there automated rollback?
[07:16] Maya: We have rollout policies: canary, A/B, automatic fallback to previous variant if quality regression triggers. Quality checks tie into your eval sets or Redwood-provided regression monitors.
[07:28] Priya: Back to networking: for PrivateLink we pay per ENI and per GB — do you have a cost model for high-throughput workloads?
[07:36] Jonas: We provided a spreadsheet in the deal folder with rough numbers, but the big cost in Dedicated is the GPU runtime; PrivateLink costs are usually a smaller portion. For tens of TBs of egress, you should estimate ENI + data transfer; we'll refine with your expected throughput.
[07:52] Aisha: For our compliance we'd like all audit logs shipped to our S3, can the Redwood agent push logs to our buckets inside the VPC?
[07:59] Ethan: Yes, for Private we can configure logging to your S3 via VPC endpoints, and send audit logs and usage events. We also support KMS for envelope encryption keys that you control.
[08:12] Priya: One of our main concerns is bursting behavior — if we see a sudden spike in traffic, how does the runtime behave with short-lived connections behind our NAT?
[08:22] Maya: Short-lived connections increase TCP handshake churn and can starve the batching pipeline. We recommend long-lived keepalives and connection pooling. If your proxy terminates keepalives or your NAT times out too aggressively, you should tune idle timeouts. We'll include recommended TCP/Metrics settings.
[08:40] Marcus: Any constraints for on-prem or air-gapped? We have one site that is air-gapped but will accept compute appliances.
[08:48] Jonas: For on-prem we provide a package and an offline installer. Control plane calls can be proxied through a customer-managed gateway or via an approved outbound channel. In air-gapped mode we ship model artifacts via secure transfer and use local KMS/HSM. We'll need to coordinate with your security team.
[09:05] Priya: Can the runtime still do auto-scaling in a private VPC?
[09:10] Maya: Yes, but you have to expose the control endpoints for autoscaler or run an internal autoscaler. For Dedicated we can run autoscaling agents in your VPC that communicate over PrivateLink.
[09:20] Ethan: Okay, let's walk through a concrete example — 100 RPS of 2k tokens, p50 target 120ms. What do we do?
[09:28] Jonas: Baseline: pick a quantized variant for throughput, set batching max to 8, latency floor at 100ms, ensure KV cache prefixing is enabled, and keep connections internal (no NAT). Use peering inside the AZ to minimize cross-AZ hops.
[09:44] Aisha: If we can't avoid the NAT for some control traffic, can we pin certain calls to bypass NAT?
[09:50] Maya: You can set route tables so internal IPs go direct and only external egress hits NAT. For more granular control use PrivateLink for control-plane endpoints and keep inference RPCs inside the VPC.
[10:03] Priya: Let's talk about TLS and cert rotation — how is that handled for PrivateLink ENIs or peered endpoints?
[10:10] Ethan: We support mTLS with cert rotation via Redwood's CA or you can supply your own. For PrivateLink we recommend mTLS plus endpoint policies. For peering, you get internal TLS between services and certs managed by our agent; rotation can be automated with your KMS/HSM.
[10:25] [10:25] Marcus: Does Redwood require any specific kernel or iptables settings on our proxies?
[10:30] Maya: Not specific kernel versions, but we recommend tuning TCP TIME_WAIT reuse, keepalive intervals, and max open files on proxies. We'll provide a hardened checklist.
[10:40] Priya: Can the Redwood runtime push metrics to our Prometheus/Grafana inside the VPC?
[10:45] Jonas: Yes, we can export metrics via Pushgateway or we can scrape an internal endpoint. Many customers run an internal Prometheus that scrapes Redwood metrics behind the VPC.
[10:55] Aisha: If we use Route53 Resolver forwarding, will Redwood be able to resolve customer-internal hostnames during fetches?
[11:02] Maya: Yes, with conditional forwarding or inbound endpoints we can resolve internal names. We'll show config examples: resolver rules, target IPs, and security group layouts.
[11:15] Priya: Any gotchas with Security Groups for PrivateLink? Our infra team is strict and tries to lock down Egress rules.
[11:22] Ethan: For PrivateLink you'll need to allow the interface ENIs to communicate on the required ports (typically 443) and the inbound SG should allow the client's subnets. We provide a minimal SG template. Also be mindful of source/dest checks on ENIs; PrivateLink handles that but for EC2 targets you may need adjustments.
[11:43] Marcus: We have a question on TLS termination — can Redwood terminate TLS for incoming requests or must it be mutual termination?
[11:50] Maya: You can choose. We support mTLS end-to-end for maximum security. If you prefer TLS termination at a customer-managed proxy with internal plaintext, that's supported too but not recommended for sensitive workloads.
[12:05] Jonas: Let's capture a quick performance example from our internal bench: same model, same hardware; peered traffic with no NAT gave p50=85ms, p95=140ms, p99=220ms at 120 RPS with batching=8. PrivateLink setup increased p50 by ~10-12ms and p99 by ~15-25ms in our environment, mostly due to extra ENI hop and endpoint processing. Your mileage varies.
[12:30] Priya: Can we tune to reduce p99 by adding more replicas?
[12:35] Jonas: Yes, horizontal scaling reduces queueing tail latency; faster autoscale and pre-warmed replicas reduce p99 substantially. We recommend a hybrid of buffer capacity and autoscale triggers on queue depth.
[12:50] Ethan: We're at about 30 minutes in. Quick check — are there any outstanding blockers from a security/compliance perspective?
[12:58] Marcus: We'll need the SOC2, KMS flow, and an architecture diagram showing data flow and where logs are stored. Also need confirmation on whether Redwood stores any customer plaintext content in hosted control plane for auditing.
[13:12] Ethan: We will share SOC2 and a network diagram. For Private deployments we can keep audit logs in your S3 and minimize any hosted-plane storage — we'll detail that in the security docs.
[13:24] Priya: Can we do an on-site network review? Our infra team prefers a working session when we run the benchmark.
[13:30] Jonas: Absolutely. We'll run a 2-hour benchmark, coordinate exact CIDRs, and we'll bring test scripts.
[13:36] Aisha: For the benchmark, can we toggle quantization and batching to see the tradeoffs?
[13:41] Maya: Yes, we'll run scenarios: (1) fp16 small-batch low latency, (2) int8 big-batch high throughput, (3) mixed with prefix/KV warm caching. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token/sec and GPU utilization.
[13:58] Priya: On the subject of routing policies, can Redwood automatically fallback to hosted if private capacity is exhausted?
[14:04] Ethan: Yes, we support automated fallback/routing rules. That said you need to agree on data residency/privacy policy for fallback. We'll show configs for route priority and tagging.
[14:18] Marcus: If fallback routes to hosted, does data leave our VPC?
[14:23] Jonas: By default yes; you can restrict fallback only to sanitized or redacted requests, or turn it off. This is configurable per route.
[14:34] Priya: Any final networking gotchas we should be aware of?
[14:38] Maya: A few: keep NAT out of hot paths, tune TCP keepalive, provision multiple AZ endpoints to avoid single AZ interruptions, pre-warm replicas for expected bursts, and use resolver endpoints to avoid DNS leaking to public.
[14:55] Ethan: Ok next steps recap — we'll share diagrams, SOC2, a network checklist, rough cost spreadsheet, and propose three 2-hour benchmark slots.
[15:05] Priya: Sounds good. Marcus and I will pull CIDR ranges and security constraints and send by next Wednesday.
[15:10] Ethan: Great. Anything else?
[15:12] Aisha: One micro question — does Redwood's agent require docker on hosts or can it run as a systemd service?
[15:18] Maya: Our agent can run containerized or as systemd; for air-gapped customers we ship RPMs/debs.
[15:24] Priya: Ok, thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email.
[15:28] Ethan: Thanks folks, we'll upload notes and set up the benchmark cadence. Bye.
